subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Sensory Cortex, Spinal Cord External Features

questions.text: Describe the external features of the spinal cord, including its enlargements and nerve attachments.
questions.explanation: The spinal cord displays cervical and lumbar enlargements corresponding to limb innervation.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord anatomy reflects peripheral nerve distribution.
questions.modelAnswer:
External features:
- Length: ~45cm in males, ~42cm in females.
- Extends from upper border of atlas vertebra (foramen magnum) to lower border of L1 vertebra.
- Enlargements:
  1. Cervical enlargement (C4-T1): Innervates upper limbs via brachial plexus.
  2. Lumbar enlargement (T11-L1): Innervates lower limbs via lumbosacral plexus.
- Conus medullaris: Tapering lower end.
- Filum terminale: Thread-like extension of pia mater anchoring cord to coccyx.

subjects.name: Histology
subjects.lectures: Structure of CNS

questions.text: Which type of neuroglial cell is responsible for forming myelin sheaths in the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons inside the CNS, while Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PNS.
questions.keyConcept: CNS myelin is formed by oligodendrocytes.

subjects.name: Biochemistry
subjects.lectures: Ammonia and Urea Cycle, Energy Sources of CNS, Hyperammonaemia, Inborn Errors of Amino Acid Metabolism, Neurotransmitters, One-carbon Unit and Folate Metabolism, Vitamin Deficiency and Metabolic Disorders

questions.text: What is the primary metabolic fuel source utilized by the brain during normal, fed states?
questions.explanation: Glucose is the primary fuel source for the brain. Ketone bodies are used only during prolonged starvation.
questions.keyConcept: Glucose is the mandatory energy substrate for the brain under normal conditions.

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Processing of Signals in CNS

questions.text: Which process describes the addition of post-synaptic potentials from multiple different synapses occurring at the same time?
questions.explanation: Spatial summation occurs when multiple presynaptic inputs release neurotransmitters simultaneously at different locations on the post-synaptic membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Spatial summation combines signals from separate synapses.

chapters.title: The Sensory System
chapters.subtitle: Receptors, Coding, Spinal Cord Internal structure and Pain Pathways

subjects.name: Histology
subjects.lectures: Gray Matter, Receptors

questions.text: Which encapsulated sensory receptor is primarily responsible for detecting low-frequency vibration and light touch?
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles detect light touch and low-frequency vibration. Pacinian corpuscles detect high-frequency vibration and pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner corpuscles serve tactile sensation.

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Pain and Pain Control, Sensation Carried by Dorsal Column Tracts, Sensations Carried by Spinothalamic Tract, Sensory Receptors and Sensory Coding, Somatosensory Cortex

questions.text: Which sensory pathway is responsible for carrying fine touch, proprioception, and vibration sensation?
questions.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception. The spinothalamic pathway carries pain and temperature.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal columns transmit epicritic sensations.

subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Ascending Pathways

questions.text: Enumerate the three neurons involved in the spinothalamic pathway carrying pain and temperature from the limbs.
questions.explanation: The spinothalamic pathway is a three-neuron chain that crosses in the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: First, second, and third-order neurons in pain pathways.
questions.modelAnswer:
Neurons of spinothalamic tract:
1. First-order neuron: Pseudounipolar neurons in the dorsal root ganglion; their central axons enter the spinal cord and synapse in the substantia gelatinosa.
2. Second-order neuron: Neurons in the substantia gelatinosa; their axons cross the midline in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the lateral spinothalamic tract to the thalamus.
3. Third-order neuron: Neurons in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus; their axons project to the primary somatosensory cortex.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Opioids

questions.text: Which opioid receptor subtype is primarily responsible for the analgesic effects as well as respiratory depression and addiction?
questions.explanation: Mu (μ) receptors mediate the majority of analgesic, respiratory-depressive, and euphoric/addictive properties of opioids.
questions.keyConcept: Mu receptor activation leads to analgesia and respiratory depression.

questions.text: Where do the majority of the fibers of the lateral corticospinal tract decussate?
questions.explanation: Approximately 85% of corticospinal fibers cross the midline in the decussation of pyramids located in the lower medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal decussation occurs in the caudal medulla.
options: Decussation of pyramids in the medulla

subjects.name: Histology
subjects.lectures: Cerebellum, Stretch Receptors, White Matter

questions.text: Which specialized muscle fibers inside a muscle spindle are innervated by gamma motor neurons?
questions.explanation: Intrafusal muscle fibers are located inside the muscle spindle and receive motor innervation from gamma motor neurons. Extrafusal fibers are innervated by alpha motor neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Intrafusal fibers regulate stretch receptor sensitivity.

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Basal Ganglia, Cerebellum, Descending Motor Tracts Functions, Motor Cortex Function, Muscle Stretch Reflex, Other Reflexes, Sensory and Motor Disorders

questions.text: Which part of the cerebellum is mainly responsible for planning, initiating, and timing of voluntary movements?
questions.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum (neocerebellum) is involved in planning, programming, and timing of motor sequences.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebrocerebellum regulates motor planning.

subjects.name: Pathology
subjects.lectures: Cerebellar Tumours, Neurodegenrative disorders of the basal ganglia

questions.text: Describe the macroscopic and microscopic pathological findings in the brain of a patient with Parkinson's disease.
questions.explanation: Parkinson's is marked by loss of pigmentation in the substantia nigra and Lewy body inclusions.
questions.keyConcept: Loss of dopaminergic pigmented neurons in substantia nigra is pathognomonic.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pathology of Parkinson's:
- Macroscopic: Pallor/loss of pigmentation in the substantia nigra (midbrain) and locus coeruleus.
- Microscopic:
  1. Severe loss of pigmented, dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra.
  2. Lewy bodies: Eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions containing alpha-synuclein in surviving neurons.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Drug Therapy of Parkinsonism

questions.text: Why is Carbidopa administered in combination with Levodopa in Parkinsonian therapy?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa is a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor. It prevents peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, reducing side effects and increasing Levodopa entry to the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa optimizes Levodopa delivery to the CNS.

subjects.name: Neurology
subjects.lectures: Clinical Applications on motor and Sensory Lesions

questions.text: Describe the clinical presentation of Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection).
questions.explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome features ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, with contralateral pain/temp loss.
questions.keyConcept: Asymmetric cord lesions present with dissociated sensory loss.
questions.modelAnswer:
Brown-Séquard presentation:
- Ipsilateral (same side) changes:
  1. Spastic paralysis below the level of lesion (corticospinal tract).
  2. Loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception below the lesion (dorsal columns).
- Contralateral (opposite side) changes:
  1. Loss of pain and temperature sensation starting 1-2 segments below the lesion (crossed spinothalamic tract).

questions.text: Which cranial nerve emerges from the posterior (dorsal) aspect of the brain stem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal aspect of the brain stem.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV dorsal brainstem emergence.

subjects.name: Histology
subjects.lectures: Medulla, Midbrain, Pons

questions.text: Which histological structure in the midbrain contains melanin granules and is severely affected in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra contains dopaminergic neurons rich in neuromelanin pigment granules.
questions.keyConcept: Pigmented midbrain substantia nigra.

chapters.title: Anatomy of the Neck
chapters.subtitle: Neck Fascia, Triangles, Cervical Plexus, and last Cranial Nerves

subjects.name: Anatomy of The Neck
subjects.lectures: Fascia, Last four cranial nerves, Suprahyoid muscles, cervical plexus and sympathetic chain, Triangles

questions.text: List the boundaries and main contents of the carotid triangle of the neck.
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle contains key neurovascular elements including the common carotid artery.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid triangle boundaries and carotid sheath contents.
questions.modelAnswer:
Boundaries:
- Anterosuperiorly: Posterior belly of digastric muscle.
- Anteroinferiorly: Superior belly of omohyoid muscle.
- Posteriorly: Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Contents:
- Carotid sheath containing:
  1. Common carotid artery (bifurcating into internal and external carotids).
  2. Internal jugular vein.
  3. Vagus nerve (CN X).
- Ansa cervicalis (embedded on the sheath).
- Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) crossing superiorly.

subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, and Third Ventricle

questions.text: Which thalamic nucleus acts as the primary relay station for visual sensory information?
questions.explanation: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) relays visual information. The medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) relays auditory info.
questions.keyConcept: LGN = Light/Vision; MGN = Music/Hearing.

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Reticular Formation, Sleep & EEG Brain Activity

questions.text: Which EEG wave pattern is typically recorded in a normal, awake adult with eyes closed and in a relaxed state?
questions.explanation: Alpha waves (8-13 Hz) are characteristic of relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed. Beta waves occur during active mental concentration with eyes open.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha rhythm denotes relaxed wakefulness.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Sedatives, Anesthetics, Epilepsy and Migraine Drugs

questions.text: Which molecular mechanism explains how Benzodiazepines exert their sedative/hypnotic effects?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines bind to GABAA receptors, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, which hyperpolarizes and inhibits the post-synaptic neuron.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepines facilitate GABA action by increasing channel opening frequency.
options: Increase frequency of GABAA channel opening
Increase duration of GABAA channel opening

chapters.subtitle: Hemisphere dominance, Speech/Aphasia, Memory, Limbic System, and Blood supply

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Speech/Aphasia, Limbic Functions, Memory and Learning

questions.text: Compare between Broca's aphasia and Wernicke's aphasia in terms of lesion location and speech features.
questions.explanation: Broca's is non-fluent motor aphasia; Wernicke's is fluent sensory aphasia.
questions.keyConcept: Expressive vs. receptive speech deficits.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Broca's Aphasia | Wernicke's Aphasia |
|---|---|---|
| Lesion site | Inferior frontal gyrus (Area 44/45) | Superior temporal gyrus (Area 22) |
| Type | Motor / Expressive / Non-fluent | Sensory / Receptive / Fluent |
| Speech production | Slow, effortful, halting, telegram-like | Rapid, fluent, but meaningless ('word salad') |
| Comprehension | Intact | Impaired |

subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Limbic Anatomy, Ventricles, CSF, Meninges, and Blood Supply

questions.text: Which blood vessel is most commonly ruptured in epidural hematomas following head trauma?
questions.explanation: Epidural hematomas are typically caused by trauma to the temple, leading to rupture of the middle meningeal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery rupture causes epidural bleed.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Antidepressants

questions.text: Which class of antidepressants works by selectively inhibiting the reuptake of serotonin without affecting norepinephrine?
questions.explanation: SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) specifically block serotonin reuptake. SNRIs block both serotonin and norepinephrine.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin availability.

chapters.subtitle: Meningitis, Poliomyelitis, Rabies, Parasitic Infections, and pathology

subjects.name: Microbiology
subjects.lectures: Bacterial, Fungal, and Viral Meningitis, Encephalitis, and Rabies

questions.text: Which laboratory parameter is classic in CSF analysis of bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis shows high polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), very low glucose (bacteria consume it), and high protein.
questions.keyConcept: Low glucose and high neutrophils in CSF indicate bacterial origin.
options: Low glucose, high protein, neutrophil predominance
Normal glucose, high protein, lymphocyte predominance
Low glucose, normal protein, eosinophil predominance
High glucose, low protein, no cells

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Treatment of Meningitis

questions.text: Which antibiotic is empirically used first-line for suspected bacterial meningitis because of its excellent CSF penetration?
questions.explanation: Third-generation cephalosporins (like Ceftriaxone or Cefotaxime) provide excellent coverage and CSF penetration for empiric meningitis therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Empiric meningitis coverage requires blood-brain barrier penetration.

subjects.name: Parasitology
subjects.lectures: Amoebic Encephalitis & Larvae affecting Brain

questions.text: Which free-living amoeba is the causative agent of rapidly fatal Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) acquired from warm fresh water?
questions.explanation: Naegleria fowleri causes Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM), entering via the olfactory neuroepithelium.
questions.keyConcept: Naegleria fowleri is the 'brain-eating' amoeba.

subjects.name: Pathology
subjects.lectures: Pathology of CNS Infections

questions.text: The presence of Negri bodies in histological sections of cerebellar Purkinje cells is diagnostic for which infection?
questions.explanation: Negri bodies are eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons infected with the Rabies virus.
questions.keyConcept: Negri bodies = Rabies virus.

subjects.name: Pathology
subjects.lectures: Neurodegenerative, Myelin, Trauma, Vascular, and CNS Tumors

questions.text: Which demyelinating disease of the CNS is characterized histologically by multiple plaques of demyelination showing oligodendrocyte loss and astrocytic proliferation?
questions.explanation: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease presenting with plaques of myelin loss throughout the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: MS plaques exhibit demyelination and axonal preservation.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Treatment of Degenerative and Myelin Diseases

questions.text: Which drug class is used to treat acute exacerbations of Multiple Sclerosis to reduce inflammation?
questions.explanation: High-dose intravenous corticosteroids (such as Methylprednisolone) are the standard first-line treatment for acute MS relapses.
questions.keyConcept: Glucocorticoids accelerate recovery in acute MS flare-ups.

subjects.name: Psychiatry
subjects.lectures: Dementia Types & Clinical Considerations

questions.text: Compare between Alzheimer's dementia and Vascular dementia in terms of onset and clinical progression.
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's is gradual and progressive, whereas Vascular dementia has a stepwise decline.
questions.keyConcept: Dementia progression shapes help define underlying etiology.
questions.modelAnswer:
Comparison:
- Alzheimer's Disease:
  - Onset: Insidious and gradual.
  - Progression: Slow, continuous, and steady decline.
  - Pathophysiology: Neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein) and senile amyloid plaques.
- Vascular Dementia:
  - Onset: Abrupt (often post-stroke) or gradual.
  - Progression: Stepwise decline with periods of stability followed by sudden drops in function.
  - Pathophysiology: Multiple cerebral infarctions or chronic microvascular ischemic injury.

chapters.title: Miscellaneous and Embryology

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Antipsychotics & Drug Abuse

questions.text: Which side effect of typical antipsychotics is characterized by involuntary, repetitive movements (like tongue protrusion and lip smacking) after long-term use?
questions.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia is a late-occurring extrapyramidal side effect caused by upregulation of dopamine receptors after chronic blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Tardive dyskinesia is associated with long-term dopamine antagonist therapy.

subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Development of Face, Nervous System, and Pharyngeal Arches

questions.text: Failure of which embryological process leads to the formation of a cleft lip?
questions.explanation: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and the medial nasal prominence on one or both sides.
questions.keyConcept: Cleft lip is a failure of maxillary and medial nasal prominence fusion.
options: Failure of maxillary and medial nasal prominence fusion
Failure of lateral nasal and maxillary prominence fusion
